chapters.title: Chapter 22. The Five on a Screen.
Chapter 24. The Cohort in Tarpon Springs.

spans.text: The ferry slowed coming into Pothia harbor and Athena saw the town for the first time and was angry that it was beautiful. The water at the harbor mouth was the strange pale blue of a Dodecanese August afternoon, and the limestone slope above the town was the color of bone where the sun fell on it and the color of old bronze where it did not, and the bell towers stood up between the white-and-pink houses like a thing the town had decided long ago.

She had been awake for nineteen hours. Tarpon Springs to Tampa, Tampa to JFK, JFK to Athens, Athens to Kos, Kos to Pothia. The last leg had been a four-hour ferry from Mastichari port that her mother had described over the phone as a short hop, the way her mother described all distances that were not the one between their kitchen and St. Nicholas Cathedral. The sea between Kos and Kalymnos had been the wrong color. Too pale. Too clear. Tarpon Springs water was warm and brown at the dock and green a mile out and the color of weak coffee in the channels. This water looked like glass somebody had polished for nothing.

The buildings on the slope above the harbor were white and pink and the saturated yellow of a school marker. Bell towers stuck up between them. Higher up, the limestone took over and a kastro sat on a ridge looking down at the boats. The boats in the harbor were smaller than the sponge boats at home, cleaner, with newer paint, and no winches she recognized. The sponge dock was somewhere else. She could feel that by the way the ferry angled in.
A man with a cardboard sign that said KDHP in green marker was waiting at the bottom of the ramp.

He was not what she had pictured. The website photos had been older. This person was barely older than she was, in a faded T-shirt and the kind of shorts you wore on a fishing boat and canvas sneakers that had been white once. He was holding the sign in one hand and a bottle of water in the other and he was not smiling.
Markou,
he said when she came down the ramp. He had spotted her before she had spotted him.
How did you know.
Last person off.
I had a big bag.
I see the bag.
He did not move toward her bag. He put the bottle of water in her hand instead.
Drink that. It’s hotter on the walk than it looks. Stelios.
Athena.
I know your name. That’s why I made the sign.

She drank the water. He watched her drink it the way you watch a kid take medicine. When she handed back the bottle he capped it and put it in a string bag over his shoulder and picked up her suitcase by the handle, not the wheels, and started walking up the harbor road. She had to half-run for two seconds to catch him.
You speak English.
I speak English.
My Greek is okay.
We’ll see.

The harbor road climbed. Ticket office. Tackle shop. A cafe with men in plastic chairs and small white coffees in tinted glass. They all turned to look at her. One said something to Stelios in Greek. She caught most of it. He answered without slowing.
What did he say.
He asked who you were.
What did you say.
I said you were Markou from Tarpon Springs.
And.
And he said kalos irthe.
Welcome. She knew the word. She had said it a thousand times at the cathedral. The man had not said it to her. He had said it to Stelios about her, which was not the same thing.

They climbed a side lane that broke off the harbor road and got steeper and shadier and quieter. Whitewashed two-story houses, iron balconies, shutters in two colors of blue. A cat watched them from a step. A scooter went past on the cross-street below and the noise bounced off the walls and went away in a second. Her suitcase wheel banged on the stone every few feet because Stelios was carrying it by the handle.
You can wheel that, I think.
It’s three more lanes.
Why are you carrying it by the handle.
Because the wheels are for airports.

He did not explain. He kept walking. She did not argue further because she did not have the air to argue. The bag on her shoulder weighed more than the suitcase. The medallion her grandmother had pinned to her shirt under the collar was sticking to her neck.

They turned onto a third lane that was wider, blue-shaded by an awning across two buildings, and stopped at a whitewashed door with a small brass plate beside it. The plate had nothing on it. It had been polished where the screws were, the way you polish around a thing you have decided not to read anymore.
This is the house.
Okay.
Five bedrooms. Kitchen. Courtyard at the back. Storage in the basement, not for you. The rules go on the fridge. The fridge is in the kitchen. The kitchen is the first door on the right.

He unlocked the door and pushed it open and held it for her. She stepped in. The entrance hall was tiled in a black-and-white pattern she had seen in old houses on St. James Street at home. The wall on her left had a row of hooks and three jackets that did not belong to her. The wall on her right had a small framed photograph she did not stop to look at. The corridor went back to a doorway with bright light beyond it. Somebody was playing a piano. The same five notes over and over with one mistake in the same place each time.
Who is that.
Phaedon. He is from Athens. He arrived a week ago and the piano was under a tarp. The tarp is no longer on the piano.
You said Athens.
He is from Athens. He is also from Alexandria, but his family has been in Athens since 1962.
Alexandria, Egypt.
Alexandria, Egypt.
Okay.
He put her suitcase down at the foot of the stairs. He took his string bag off his shoulder and hung it on a hook. He looked at her the way he had looked at her drinking the water at the harbor.

Phaedon is in the second-floor bedroom on the courtyard side. Niko is in the harbor-side single at the top of the stairs. Lina is in the room next to Niko. You are in the room across from Lina, on the harbor side. Tia is in the room next to Phaedon.
Tia is already here.
Tia came in on the eighteenth. Phaedon came in two days before her. You are the last.
I had connections.
Everyone had connections.

He counted the rooms on his fingers as if she had not been listening. She had been listening. She was tired and she was thirsty and she was standing in the entrance hall of a house she had imagined every night for a year, and the photograph she had not looked at on the right-hand wall was at the edge of her vision and the patient slow piano playing badly somewhere behind a closed door was filling up the parts of her brain she had been planning to use to be impressive.
Which room is the larger one.
The harbor-side double.
And who is in that one.

Nobody. The double is the shared sitting room on the second floor. It used to be a bedroom in the 1920s. It is not a bedroom now. The rooms you are getting are the rooms you are getting. We do them in order of arrival. Phaedon had the courtyard-side single because he wanted to be away from the harbor wall. The harbor wall is the one with salt damage. Niko took the bathroom-side bedroom because he wanted the shorter walk in the morning. Lina took the room next to Niko because Niko asked her to. You are across from Lina because that is the room that was left.
Niko asked her to.
He asked her quietly. They had not spoken to each other before that. She said yes.
I have salt damage.

You have a perfectly good room with the harbor view. The salt damage is on the bedroom wall by the bed. The wall is over a hundred years old and the harbor has been there longer. The wall takes the weather. My room has it. Tia’s has it. Lina’s has it. Niko’s does not. He won that.
By being polite.
By being there first and by asking quietly. You can ask quietly later. The harbor-side single is what is left today.
The piano stopped. A woman’s voice from somewhere above her, on the stairs, slow and unbothered.
Stelios.
Tia.
There is a bee in the bathroom.
There is always a bee in the bathroom.
You said you would fix the window.
I said I would put the screen in. The window is fine.
The screen is on the kitchen table.
Then put the screen in the window.
You are taller.

Athena turned to find the voice. The girl at the top of the stairs was almost her age and was barefoot and was wearing a man’s button-down shirt over an old swim top. She had her hair tied back with a rubber band. She held the screen by one corner. She nodded at Athena the way you nod at somebody whose name you already know.
Markou.
Yeah.
Tia.
Tia, hi.
Hi. Stelios will not fix the bee.
I will fix the bee,
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Stelios said.
Bring me the screen.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Tia came down the stairs the way somebody who had walked a sandy beach since she was four years old comes down stairs. The screen went past Athena and into Stelios’s hand and Tia kept going past her into the kitchen without stopping. She had looked at Athena’s face for two seconds and at her bag for one second and at the entrance-hall floor on the way past, and Athena had felt all three lookings without being able to say what she had been measured for.
Stelios carried the screen toward the bathroom. He stopped before the bathroom door.
The photograph on the wall behind you. There is a label. You should read it later. Not now. You have not eaten and you are about to lose your temper. Read it tomorrow.
What.

The photograph. There is a label tucked behind the glass. The name on the label includes a Markou. There are Markous in Kalymnos. There are Markous on every Greek island that ever sent anybody anywhere. You will want to know about it. You will be wrong about most of what you guess. Wait until tomorrow.
He went into the bathroom. The door closed. The bee buzzed once on the inside of the door and went quiet.
Athena turned to the photograph.

It was a sepia print in a wooden frame the size of a paperback. A family stood on the front step of a house. The house was the same house. She recognized the door behind them. She recognized the lintel. She recognized the iron knocker in the shape of a hand, which she had not until this second realized she had walked under.

Two adults and four children. The adults were a man in a high-collared suit and a woman in a long dress with a sash. The children were in white. The smallest was holding a sponge bigger than her head and looking at the sponge. The other three were looking at the camera. The taller of the three was a girl of about thirteen, in a white dress with a darker ribbon at the waist.
The plate on the bottom of the frame said Drosos family, August 1922 in English and in Greek.
There was a slip of paper tucked behind the glass, against the inside edge of the wooden frame. She tilted the frame to read it. The pencil writing was old and even.
Eleni, Stamatis, Maria, Despina, Manolis, Markou Drosos.
She read the line twice. She felt the heat in her ears before she felt anything else.
She turned and walked into the kitchen.

It was a long room with a stone floor and a green-painted dresser along one wall and a kitchen table in the middle the size of a boat door. Phaedon was at the stove with his back to her. He was tall and thin and had the kind of skin that did not redden in heat. He had a kitchen towel over one shoulder and the smell coming off the pan was lemon and garlic and oil and an herb she did not know. Tia was at the table cutting cucumbers into a bowl with a small knife, without looking at the cucumbers. Both of them looked up.
You arrived,
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: Phaedon said.
I arrived.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Stelios is doing the rooms thing.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: He told me the rooms thing.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: I told him it was a stupid way to do it. He said it was the program’s rules. I checked. It is not the program’s rules. It is Stelios’s rule.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: That is consistent,
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Tia said.
With Stelios.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Hi,
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: Phaedon said.
Phaedon.
Athena.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: He did not put his hand out. He did not move from the stove. He looked at her face for slightly longer than was comfortable. He nodded once.
There is iced tea in the fridge. Stelios’s mother makes it. She makes it without sugar and with cinnamon. Drink one or drink three. Do not drink two.
Why.
Because if you drink three you will have a headache by sundown and you will blame Greece. If you drink one you will be fine. Two is the bad number. Trust me.
Tia made a soft sound that was almost a laugh and went back to cutting cucumbers.

Athena went to the fridge. The fridge was full in the way that a fridge a week into five people living together is full. She found the pitcher. She poured a glass. She drank half. The tea was the color of weak black coffee and tasted like a country she had not been to.
Who were the Drosos family.

Phaedon put the wooden spoon down on the rest. Tia did not look up. Neither was suddenly moving slowly. Both were already doing the slow work that people do when a question they are not sure who should answer enters the room.
They owned this house,
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: Phaedon said.
I gathered.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Sponge merchants. From the late nineteenth century. The last Drosos died in 2019. The house came to the foundation in 2024.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: There’s a photograph of them in the entrance hall.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: There are photographs of them all through the house. The foundation has not finished cataloguing them.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: There is a name on the photograph in the entrance hall.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Many names.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: My name.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Phaedon looked at Tia. Tia looked at the cucumber she was halfway through cutting. She put the knife down. She wiped her hands on the front of her shirt without ceremony, lifted her face, and looked at Athena directly.
Sit down a minute.
I’d rather stand.
Sit down a minute anyway.
Athena sat. She put her glass in front of her. Tia sat across.
There are families in Kalymnos with the same surname as families in Tarpon Springs,
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Tia said.

It is not unusual. The diaspora started here. The name on the photograph is a Drosos who married into a Markou family in 1922. Stelios told me on my second day. He is not hiding it. He told you to wait because you have been on planes for a day. There are records at the museum. We can walk you there. We have walked there three times already. Phaedon is interning at the museum and has read most of it. Lina has read the rest. We are not keeping anything from you. We are trying not to land a hundred years of family history on you in your first hour. Sit. Drink the tea. Eat something.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: She said it without sharpness. She said it the way you tell a person a thing she will need to understand for years.
Athena did not say anything for a long while. Tia did not look away. Phaedon, at the counter, turned the stove back on under the pan and stirred without watching what he was doing.
Okay.
Okay.
I’ll wait until tomorrow.
Wait until you’ve eaten.
Wait until I’ve eaten.
Wait until you’ve eaten.
Phaedon, at the stove, said something in Greek so quietly Athena was not certain he had said it to anyone. Tia heard it and the corner of her mouth went up half a millimeter and then back down.

Somebody came in through the courtyard door at the back of the kitchen behind a beaded curtain Athena had not noticed before. The beads parted. A girl came in with a market bag over one shoulder and the kind of compass on a string that you actually used, around her neck. She had short hair, dark, and the air of having walked from somewhere precise to somewhere precise. She set the bag on the counter without looking at Athena and pulled a kilo of tomatoes out by the stem. Then she turned.
You arrived.
Hi.
Lina.
Athena.
I know.

She nodded once and went to the sink and washed her hands. The hands were small and careful. She had a watch on her left wrist that did not match the rest of her. Phaedon, at the stove, said something to her in Greek. She answered in French. He laughed. Tia, still at the table, said something in English to no one in particular.
They do this. They have done this since Lina arrived. It is amusing for the first hour.
Lina dried her hands and turned around and rested her hip against the counter and looked at Athena again. The look was longer than Tia’s and shorter than Phaedon’s.
Stelios told you about the photograph.
He told me to wait until tomorrow.

He is correct that you should wait until tomorrow. He is incorrect that the photograph is the most interesting one in the house. There are three more in the upstairs hall and one in your room. Yours is the most specific.
In my room.
Above the bed. To the right of the window. Smaller. You will see it when you go up.
You went into my room.
I helped Stelios change the sheets the morning your room was ready. I did not move the photograph. I am telling you it is there so that you do not feel ambushed.
That is not how being ambushed works.
I am telling you anyway.

Phaedon, at the stove, did not look at any of them. He stirred. The room was quiet in the way that a kitchen can be quiet while still containing four people. Athena heard the bathroom door open and Stelios came back down the corridor with the screen in his hand and the bee, apparently, no longer alive. Behind him she heard another set of footsteps, slower, coming down the stairs. The piano had been silent since Tia called Stelios about the bathroom.
Niko walked into the kitchen.

He was not what she had pictured. She had pictured an Australian. He was an Australian, but not an Australian in the way she had practiced for. He was tall and narrow and quiet. His shirt was a soft grey that had once been black. His hair was the kind of dark that did not photograph well in any light. He looked at her exactly long enough to count her as new and not long enough to make her feel watched. He had a pearl on a leather cord around his neck. The pearl sat on the cotton of his shirt the way somebody puts a thing where they want to keep noticing it.
Niko.
Athena.
Hi.
Hi.

He went to the fridge, poured half a glass of the iced tea, looked at the level, and put the pitcher back in the door. He took one swallow. He looked at the corner of the kitchen by the stove, where the wiring came down from the ceiling and ran along the molding to a junction box above the sink.
That box is loose.
I know,
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Stelios said from the doorway.
It is loose because somebody took it apart and put it back wrong. The screws are the wrong screws.
I know.
You said somebody is coming.
In the spring.
It is the wrong season for it to wait that long.
They are not coming sooner.
It is wired like somebody wanted one room dark.
I know.

Niko shrugged once. He took the second swallow of his iced tea and put the empty glass in the sink and walked back out of the kitchen the way he had walked in. The stairs creaked twice. The piano did not start again. The bathroom screen, Athena noticed, was now in the bathroom window.

Stelios came the rest of the way into the kitchen and reached up over her head and unhooked her shoulder bag from where she had not realized she had put it back on the chair behind her. He set it on the bottom of the dresser. He put a small plate in front of her with two slices of cucumber and a piece of feta and a piece of olive oil bread. He did not say anything. He walked back out toward the bathroom and shut the cabinet under the sink in there and came back through and started cutting tomatoes next to Lina.
What is for dinner,
spans.speaker: Athena

spans.text: Athena said.
Lemon chicken,
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: Phaedon said.

Rice. Cucumber. Tomato. A piece of cheese. Bread. Iced tea. Wine for the adults at the table, which is Stelios because Stelios is twenty and counts as adult on the island. Niko’s mother sent honey. We will put the honey on something.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: What time.
Eight.
Where is the bathroom.
Top of the stairs, on the left.
And the room across from Lina is which one.
Top of the stairs, on the right, second door.
I’ll take it.
Yes,
spans.speaker: Lina

spans.text: Lina said.
You will.
spans.speaker: Lina

spans.text: Athena ate the cheese and the cucumber and the bread on the small plate. She finished the tea. She picked up her shoulder bag and went out into the corridor.
She climbed the stairs. The wood of the stairs was darker than the floor of the corridor. The wall along the stairs had four more framed photographs and she did not look at any of them.

The bedroom door was open. The room was small. The bed was iron-framed and made up with a white cover and a blue cover folded at the foot. The window was open and the linen curtain was pulled back and the harbor was visible between two roofs across the lane. The salt damage was on the wall by the bed, where Stelios had said it would be, and it had bubbled the plaster into something that looked like the surface of a sponge cell.

She put her suitcase down. She put her shoulder bag down. She walked to the window. The harbor at five-thirty in the afternoon was the same wrong color as it had been from the ferry. She watched a small white boat with a blue trim cross from one end of her window to the other.
Then she turned.
The wall by the bed had a small framed photograph hanging beside the headboard. She had not noticed it from the door. She walked over and looked at it.

A girl in a white dress with a dark ribbon at the waist, on the front step of a house, holding a sponge. The same girl as the entrance hall, but younger. The print was smaller. The plate on the bottom of the frame said Despina, 1919.
She lifted the frame off the nail and turned it over.
On the back, in pencil, in a hand a hundred years old, the inscription read:
Despina, my brother’s daughter. Pothia. Before America.

She read it twice. She put the frame back on the nail with both hands so it did not knock against the plaster. She sat down on the bed. The mattress was firmer than the bed at home. The light through the window was the same color as the light in the photograph.

Downstairs, somebody opened the courtyard door and somebody else laughed once and the beads went chattering. Lina said something to Phaedon in French and Phaedon answered in Greek. Stelios said something in Kalymniko that Athena half-caught. Niko said nothing. The kettle came on.

Athena reached into the collar of her shirt and unpinned her grandmother’s medallion and held it in her palm. The medallion was warm from her skin. Saint Nicholas on the front. Her grandmother’s initials on the back. D. M., 1962. Her grandmother had been seventeen the year she had received it. The same age Athena was now.
She closed her hand around it.

She did not yet know what to do with what she had seen on the back of the photograph. She did not yet know whether to tell anyone. She did not yet know whether Lina had read it before her, or whether Stelios had, or whether her grandmother in Tarpon Springs had known about it her whole life and had never said the word. She did not yet know that the photograph in the entrance hall would be the one she would not look at for fifteen months, or that a ledger on a shelf at the museum down the lane would be at her hand by January. She did not need to know.
She knew she was not going to call her grandmother tonight.

She lay back on the bed for a moment and watched the ceiling. The ceiling had a small water stain in one corner shaped like a country she could not name. Below her, in the kitchen, a chair scraped and a glass set down and a knife went into a board. The piano started again. Different hand this time. Faster and more sure of itself. A melody she had heard once at her grandmother’s house and could not place.
She closed her eyes.
The medallion warmed in her palm.
She let the day land.
